question: What does a professional review and refactoring of a real, well-regarded open-source class (JCommon's SerialDate) look like, step by step?
contributions: A worked refactoring of SerialDate into DayDate: first make it work (tests), then make it right, annotated with smell/heuristic codes [C1], [G5], [N1] etc. that point to the book's ch. 17 catalogue

results.claim: The original unit tests covered only about half of SerialDate's executable statements (Clover).
results.setup: SerialDate in JCommon, original SerialDateTests, measured with Clover
results.quote: reported that the unit tests executed only 91 of the 185 executable statements in SerialDate

results.claim: Martin's own independent test suite raised coverage to 92 percent, even with failing tests commented out.
results.quote: executing 170 (92 percent) out of the 185 executable statements.

results.claim: After refactoring, DayDate's coverage percentage fell to 84.9 percent because the class shrank, not because less was tested; 45 of 53 statements covered, the uncovered ones judged too trivial to test.
results.quote: Interestingly the code coverage in DayDate has decreased to 84.9 percent!
results.note: the 45 of 53 figure is split across a hyphenated line break in the text

results.claim: Writing tests for behaviour the code should have exposed a boundary-condition bug in getFollowingDayOfWeek (Dec 25 2004, a Saturday, returned itself as the following Saturday); fix was changing the comparison at line 685.
results.quote: It is a typical boundary condition error [T5].

results.claim: Coverage showed one branch in getNearestDayOfWeek never ran, proving the algorithm wrong; the pattern of failing tests showed it failed when the nearest day was in the future.
Replacing int month constants with a Month enum took about an hour and removed isValidMonthCode and the month error checking.
results.setup: SerialDate to DayDate, Month enum, one author's estimate
results.quote: It took me an hour to make all the changes.

results.claim: After a chain of IDE-driven refactorings, Martin found the only callers of weekInMonthToString and relativeToString were tests, and deleted both functions and their tests.
results.quote: Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me!

limits: One class, one author's judgement; no measurement of whether the result is easier to maintain.
Martin concedes reviewers disagreed on deleting serialVersionUID (fn. 2) and admits naming choices may not suit the reader (p. 276).
Java 2008 idioms (enums, final, Javadoc, Clover); the listings use the old SerialDate names throughout.
Only a few refactored snippets are printed; full listings are in Appendix B, not in this PDF.
practices: Make it work before making it right: get tests passing and coverage high first (pp. 268-270).
Check coverage with a tool and write tests for behaviour the class should have, leaving failing ones commented until fixed (p. 268).
Run all tests after every change (p. 270).
Treat a professional code review as normal and welcome (p. 268).
Delete change-history comments, redundant comments and unused code; source control does that job (pp. 270, 272, 275).
Name at the right level of abstraction: do not let a name imply an implementation (SerialDate to DayDate) (p. 271).
Replace int constants with enums, so they are easy to rename and need no validation (pp. 271, 275-276).
Do not inherit from a constants class (p. 271).
Base classes should not know their derivatives; use Abstract Factory (p. 273).
Move members to where they are used, push down or pull up by real dependency, and watch for logical dependencies (pp. 272-275, 282).
Avoid flag arguments that select output format (p. 278).
Fix feature envy by moving methods to the class whose data they use (p. 278).
Make methods that use instance data instance methods, and rename to show immutability (addDays to plusDays) (pp. 279-280).
Use explaining temporary variables to clarify algorithms (pp. 279-281).
Remove duplication by extracting a method (correctLastDayOfMonth) (p. 283).
Delete final keywords on arguments and variables as clutter (p. 276).
Delete tests whose only subject is code you have just deleted (p. 281).
Leave the code cleaner than you found it: the Boy Scout Rule (p. 284).

terms.definition: We've checked the code in a bit cleaner than when we checked it out.
named locals that make a complicated algorithm more transparent (citing Beck97)
a method that uses another class's data more than its own, so it belongs there (citing Fowler)
pattern used to create DayDate instances and answer implementation questions without the base class knowing its derivatives (citing GOF)

lineage.note: Martin rejects its advice to use final everywhere
